overview: This 1500 to 1530 atlas label groups disconnected parts of Sind and Makran, Gujarat, and the Deccan. It is regional shorthand, not one empire or religious population. Thatta’s Samma court and neighbouring Mandu had distinct histories. Named sultanates retain their own cards; Mandu and Bidar appear below only as comparisons.

periods.title: Different courts around 1500
periods.summary: Thatta remained associated with Jam Nizamuddin’s Samma court. Its history was distinct from the other regions combined by this label.

periods.title: Books crossed political boundaries
periods.summary: In neighbouring Mandu, a Persian mechanics manuscript was copied in 1508 and checked in 1509, connecting local scholars with much older Arabic technical knowledge.

periods.title: Projects outlast the map window
periods.summary: At Burhanpur, the official monument account places Begum Rokeya’s mosque completion broadly between 1520 and 1540, extending beyond this atlas interval.

sections.title: Reading the map and its different courts

items.text: The three outlines include Thatta, Ahmedabad, Champaner and Burhanpur, but exclude Mandu, Bidar and Golconda at the sampled 1500 snapshot. Those boundaries cannot describe every Muslim-ruled territory, still less everyone’s religion. The examples below name their locations because courts, craftspeople and books belonged to overlapping regional worlds.

Thatta stood near the Indus delta and became the capital of successive Samma, Arghun and Tarkhan dynasties. Its surviving stone and brick monuments preserve several centuries of patronage. A later tomb beside an earlier one is therefore evidence of changing rulers, not a single royal family reigning throughout.

Jam Nizamuddin’s tomb at Makli makes stone look almost embroidered: lotus bands, sunflower panels, geese, miniature spires and Arabic calligraphy share its walls. Sindh’s conservation department compares the workmanship with Gujarat. Craftsmen could combine an extensive visual vocabulary within one ruler’s memorial.

At Mubarak Khan’s enclosure in Makli, inscriptions name patrons and preserve a royal genealogy, while several graves share the walled space. One entrance records construction in 1490, just before this map window. The monuments make family remembrance visible, although later completion and some relationships remain debated.

sections.title: Women, skilled work and long-distance cloth

items.text: In Ahmedabad, Bai Harir Sultani held responsibility in Sultan Mahmud Begada’s royal household and sponsored a mosque, tomb and stepwell complex. ASI dates the mosque to 1500 from its central prayer-niche inscription. A woman’s administrative position and building patronage can therefore be traced in a surviving place.

Bai Harir’s mosque has five domed bays, with the central dome raised above the others at a clerestory level. Carved columns and smaller domes also frame her tomb’s veranda. Builders arranged light, height and ornament together; the structure was more than a decorated flat room.

The nearby well also had a planted setting. Burgess’s archaeological survey translates its Arabic inscription as mentioning fruit-bearing trees beside the ornamented building. He distinguishes the Sanskrit inscription’s 1499 dating from the Arabic inscription’s 1500 date. The paired records show why a monument need not have one simple birthday.

A cotton cloth probably made in Gujarat during the 1500s shows twelve women playing stringed instruments, each with a parrot perched on one hand. Their skirts and blouses alternate red and blue. Block printing, resist dyeing and painting worked together: pattern, colour and a small musical parade on fabric.

That cloth is just over five metres long and was found on Sulawesi in Indonesia. Its old darns, newer patches and lasting fold mark reveal a life beyond manufacture. A valuable textile could cross seas and keep being repaired. Its exact travel route and arrival date are not recorded.

At Burhanpur, the National Monuments Authority credits Begum Rokeya with completing Bibi Sahib’s mosque after work began under Adil Khan III. Its broad dating, 1520 to 1540, crosses the map’s endpoint. The building extends the story of women as patrons into a different royal court.

The same Burhanpur mosque preserves two Persian inscriptions on pillars and an Arabic religious inscription over the gate. Its architectural style also reflects Gujarat. Languages and building ideas could travel without making the two courts one state. Here, the stones retain more than one kind of written voice.

sections.title: A neighbouring court’s kitchens and classrooms

items.text: Mandu lies outside these outlines, but its books offer unusually close evidence for a neighbouring sultanate around 1500. The Book of Delights began under Ghiyas al-Din and appears to have continued under Nasir Shah. One samosa recipe combines minced meat, onion, ginger and aubergine before frying the filled pastry in ghee.

Another Mandu recipe turns leftover rice-cooking water into broth with mung pulses, seasoning and mint. The manuscript illustrates preparing the rice water. Even an elaborate royal recipe collection found a use for something a hurried cook might pour away: rice-cooking liquid could have another job.

The Book of Delights gathers remedies and perfumes alongside food. It shows courtly interest in bodily care as well as taste and fragrance. Such recipes document historical practice; they do not establish that a treatment worked, or tell us what medical care an ordinary family could obtain.

Mandu’s illustrated Key of the Learned was a learning tool for moving between languages. Its text was composed in 1468 to 1469 and the surviving illustrated copy is dated around 1490, before this map window. Persian entries acquire Arabic and Hindavi equivalents, while pictures help explain objects and words.

That dictionary includes a hobbyhorse: its Hindavi name, ḍanḍā-mūhī, means “stick-face.” The scribe added dots to a Perso-Arabic letter to represent a local sound. Children’s toys entered a serious language manual. Even a pretend horse could give an adult scholar a spelling problem.

Mandu’s Wonders of Mechanics adapted al-Jazari’s Arabic engineering book into Persian for Nasir Shah. Its earliest known copy dates to 1508. Technical diagrams and local vocabulary helped readers understand mechanical devices across languages. A book explaining a machine is evidence of technical learning, not proof that every illustrated device was built there.

A Persian note in that Mandu manuscript reads, in scholarly transcription, “ṣaḥīḥ ast ghalaṭ nīst”: “It is correct; it is not incorrect.” The book was copied in 1508 and verified the following year; the note is associated with that checking by handwriting. A delightfully emphatic proofreader, preserved on paper.

Nearby Bidar, also outside this particular outline, preserves a fifteenth-century underground water system. Gently sloping tunnels carried groundwater, with vertical shafts giving access from above. Builders adapted a technique associated with Iranian migrants to local water-bearing rock: the slope, rather than an electric pump, moved the water.

Keeping those tunnels useful requires care above ground too. Modern conservation, whose planning phase ran from 2016 to 2018, addressed solid waste with filters and household rubbish collection. That is a present-day conservation lesson, not a claim about medieval toilets. Water infrastructure depends on maintenance as well as clever construction.

ending.text: There was no collective collapse of “Islamic states” in 1530. The atlas simply ends this label. Thatta later passed through Arghun and Tarkhan rule and came under Mughal government in 1592; Burhanpur’s building work continued beyond the window. Particular dynasties changed, while cities, craft traditions and multilingual communities continued.
